This is the last of four tasks building a small dependency-free text-statistics module (`src/textstats.js`, CommonJS, Node 20, `npm test` = `node --test`). - `assertText(fn, value)` throws `TypeError` with the message prefix `<fn>:` when value is not a string.

Global constraints: one test file per function (`test/readingTimeMinutes.test.js`) using `const { test } = require('node:test');` and `const assert = require('node:assert/strict');`. Test names are full present-tense sentences. Error tests assert on the error class and the message prefix only. Write the tests first, run `npm test`, and watch them fail for the stated reason before writing the implementation. Make one commit, prefixed `feat:`, with the test and implementation together, and never commit while `npm test` is red.

- D1: Build the 270-word, three-paragraph text the brief's prose describes (for example, 10 copies of a 9-word sentence across 3 paragraphs) and assert its hand-counted result in a test. Also assert `wordCount` of that text equals 270, so the fixture is proven.
- D2: Add tests for every behaviour bullet the plan's listed tests omit. This includes the wpm RangeError cases, fractional wpm, and an explicit `undefined` wpm falling back to the default. Keep the implementation code exactly as the brief gives it. Your test count may go past the plan's stated totals.

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. - Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
